claims.text: W–Ta–V–Cr is a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
The initial W–Ta–V–Cr alloy is a random solid solution.
Tailored thermomechanical processing of W–Ta–V–Cr will refine its grains.
Tailored thermomechanical processing of W–Ta–V–Cr will produce well-distributed nanoscale precipitates.
Fine grains and nanoscale precipitates in W–Ta–V–Cr will act as sinks for radiation-induced defects such as dislocation loops.
The proposed defect sinks will suppress radiation damage in W–Ta–V–Cr.
The refined microstructure will allow W–Ta–V–Cr to retain high-temperature strength during irradiation.
The hierarchical microstructure will reduce helium-bubble formation and associated surface degradation.
Microstructural refinement will help limit neutron activation of the alloy.
Engineered W–Ta–V–Cr will have better irradiation tolerance than conventional tungsten alloys.
Engineered W–Ta–V–Cr will sustain high-temperature mechanical properties better than conventional tungsten alloys.
Engineered W–Ta–V–Cr will have lower activation than conventional tungsten alloys.
Fusion plasma-facing materials must operate for long durations at temperatures of at least 1000 K while exposed to hydrogen isotopes, helium ash, and neutrons.
Tungsten is a leading plasma-facing-material candidate because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rate, and low tritium retention.
Conventional tungsten is susceptible to helium-induced bubbles, pits, holes, and related surface morphology changes.
Conventional tungsten alloys undergo significant activation under neutron irradiation.
Refractory high-entropy alloys generally have excellent elevated-temperature mechanical properties and are considered promising for advanced nuclear applications.
A hierarchically structured W–Ta–V–Cr alloy is a viable low-activation structural material for high-temperature fusion plasma-facing components.
